function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑use set of files** you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository.  
They cover:

| Section | File | Purpose |
|---------|------|---------|
| **Docker** | `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image. |
| **Kubernetes** | `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment definition. |
| | `k8s/service.yaml` | Service definition. |
| **GitHub Actions** | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes the Docker image on every push to `main`. |

> **NOTE** – The repo is assumed to contain a typical Node.js entry point (`app.js` or `index.js`) and a `package.json`.  
> If your entry point is named differently, adjust the Dockerfile’s `ENTRYPOINT` accordingly.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – lightweight Node.js runtime
FROM node:14-alpine

# Maintainer
LABEL maintainer="Unknown"

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why `node:14-alpine`?**  
> Alpine images are small (~50 MB) and work well for production Node.js workloads.  
> If you need a newer Node version, change the `FROM` line to `node:16-alpine`, etc.

---

## 2. Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a folder `k8s/` (or any name you prefer) and add the following two files.

### 2.1 `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
  labels:
    app: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: production
          resources:
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "256Mi"
            requests:
              cpu: "250m"
              memory: "128Mi"
```

### 2.2 `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deployment runs 2 replicas of your container.  
> * Service exposes them on port 80 inside the cluster, forwarding to container port 3000.  
> * Adjust `replicas`, `resources`, or `service.type` (e.g., `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`) as needed.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows/` and add `ci.yml`.

```yaml
name: CI – Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Set up Docker Buildx
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      # Log into GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io)
      - name: Log into GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build and push the image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
            ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      # Optional: Create a GitHub release (if you want to tag releases)
      # - name: Create Release
      #   uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
      #   with:
      #     tag_name: v${{ github.run_number }}
      #     generate_release_notes: true
```

> **Key points**  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication – no extra secrets required.  
> * Tags the image with `latest` and the commit SHA for traceability.  
> * If you prefer Docker Hub, replace the login and tags accordingly.

---

## 4. Commit & Push

Open a terminal in the repository root and run:

```bash
# 1. Add the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# 2. Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 3. Push to main
git push origin main
```

> **If you’re on a different branch**  
> Replace `main` with your branch name in the `push` command.

---

## 5. Verify

1. **Dockerfile** – `docker build -t test-image .` should succeed locally.  
2. **Kubernetes** – `kubectl apply -f k8s/` should create the deployment & service.  
3. **GitHub Actions** – After pushing, check the Actions tab; the workflow should run, build the image, and push it to `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome`.

---

### Quick Checklist

- [ ] Dockerfile uses `node:14-alpine` (or your preferred Node version).  
- [ ] Kubernetes deployment uses `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`.  
- [ ] Service exposes port 80 → container port 3000.  
- [ ] GitHub Actions workflow builds & pushes on `main` pushes.  
- [ ] All files added, committed, and pushed.

Happy coding! 🚀
